board_events.text: Conditional Probability — Shrinking the World
New information doesn't change reality; it changes what we know.
Given $F$ has happened, how likely is $E$ now?
$F$ is a fact you're handed — not a second event you hope for.
Top: outcomes in both $E$ and $F$. Bottom: the reduced world, just $F$.

board_events.caption: Condition on F: keep only what's inside F.

board_events.text: Valid only when $P(F) > 0$.

segments.text: <curious>Sounds simple, but this hides the whole chapter.</curious> On a Mumbai platform you guess the next train; the board flashes Western Railway and your guess sharpens. The trains didn't change — what you know did.
That's conditional probability. Information doesn't rewrite what's happening; it shrinks the possibilities you reason about down to a smaller, relevant world.
So probability of E given F asks: F has definitely occurred, and given that, how likely is E right now?
The key shift is this. F isn't a second event you also want. It's handed to you as fact, so you discard every outcome where F didn't happen.
That gives the formula: probability of E given F equals probability of E-and-F, over probability of F.
The top counts outcomes inside both E and F; the bottom is your new universe, just F. You've stopped dividing by the whole sample space.
Picture a Diwali mela. F is the food-court crowd. Told the person is there, you count jalebi-eaters among food-court people only; the rest is irrelevant.
One guard-rail: this needs probability of F above zero. You can never condition on the impossible.

<curious>Simple लगता है, पर यहीं पूरा chapter छुपा है।</curious> Mumbai platform पे तुम next train guess करते हो; board पे Western Railway चमकता है और guess sharp हो जाता है। Trains नहीं बदलीं — जो पता है वो बदला।
यही है conditional probability। Information reality नहीं बदलती; बस possibilities को एक छोटी, relevant दुनिया तक shrink कर देती है।
तो probability of E given F पूछता है: F हो चुका है, और अब E कितना likely है?
मुख्य बात ये है। F कोई दूसरा event नहीं जो तुम चाहते हो। वो fact के तौर पे दिया गया है, इसलिए हर वो outcome हटा दो जहाँ F नहीं हुआ।
इससे formula मिलता है: probability of E given F बराबर probability of E-and-F, बटा probability of F।
ऊपर वाला E और F दोनों के outcomes गिनता है; नीचे वाला तुम्हारी नई दुनिया है, सिर्फ F। अब पूरे sample space से भाग नहीं दे रहे।
Diwali mela सोचो। F है food-court की भीड़। पता चला बंदा वहीं है, तो jalebi खाने वाले सिर्फ food-court वालों में गिनो; बाकी mela irrelevant।
एक guard-rail: probability of F, zero से ऊपर होनी चाहिए। Impossible पे कभी condition नहीं कर सकते।

board_events.text: Independence — When Knowing Changes Nothing
Sometimes new information is completely useless.
Toss a coin, then roll a die: heads tells you nothing about the die.
$F$ shrank the world, but $E$'s share of it is unchanged.
Colony of 100 families: 30 own a car, 40 own a two-wheeler.

board_events.caption: Overlap size decides dependence.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 440 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="20" y="26" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#334155">Among 40 two-wheeler owners, how many own a car?</text><rect x="30" y="46" width="180" height="44" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="30" y="46" width="54" height="44" fill="#86efac" stroke="#15803d" stroke-width="2"/><text x="46" y="74" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#14532d">12</text><text x="222" y="74" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#334155">12/40 = 0.30</text><text x="30" y="108" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#15803d">independent (info useless)</text><rect x="30" y="130" width="180" height="44" fill="#e2e8f0" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="30" y="130" width="81" height="44" fill="#fca5a5" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2"/><text x="60" y="158" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#7f1d1d">18</text><text x="222" y="158" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#334155">18/40 = 0.45</text><text x="30" y="192" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#b91c1c">dependent (info helps)</text></svg>

board_events.text: Same machinery, two stories — decided by the overlap.

segments.text: Conditional probability has a twin idea, and here it is: sometimes the new information simply doesn't matter.
If knowing F leaves E exactly as likely as before, then F told you nothing useful about E. That is independence.
Toss a coin, then roll a die. Knowing the coin showed heads changes nothing about the die; the die doesn't care.
Formally, E and F are independent when probability of E given F equals the plain probability of E. The condition didn't move the number.
Notice what that means geometrically. F did shrink the world, but E's slice of that smaller world is identical to its slice of the big one.
A concrete feel. In a hundred families, thirty own a car and forty own a two-wheeler. Pick one at random and the car chance is thirty percent.
Now say twelve own both. Learn the family owns a two-wheeler: among those forty, twelve own a car, still thirty percent. Change both to eighteen and it jumps to forty-five percent.
Same setup, two different stories, decided entirely by how big the overlap is. Small overlap means independent; a larger overlap means the information starts to matter.
Conditional probability का एक twin idea है, ये रहा: कभी-कभी नई information matter ही नहीं करती।
अगर F जानने के बाद E पहले जितना ही likely रहे, तो F ने E के बारे में कुछ useful बताया ही नहीं। यही है independence।
Coin toss करो, फिर die roll। Coin पे heads आया, die के बारे में कुछ नहीं बदलता; die को फ़र्क़ ही नहीं पड़ता।
Formally, E और F independent हैं जब probability of E given F बराबर हो plain probability of E के। Condition ने number हिलाया ही नहीं।
Geometrically देखो। F ने दुनिया shrink तो की, पर उस छोटी दुनिया में E का हिस्सा बड़ी दुनिया वाले हिस्से जितना ही है।
Concrete feel। सौ families में तीस के पास car, चालीस के पास two-wheeler। एक random pick और car का chance तीस percent।
अब मानो बारह के पास दोनों हैं। पता चला family के पास two-wheeler है: उन चालीस में बारह के पास car, फिर भी तीस percent। दोनों को अठारह कर दो तो पैंतालीस percent पे कूद जाता है।
वही setup, दो अलग कहानियाँ, पूरी तरह overlap के size से तय। छोटा overlap मतलब independent; बड़ा overlap मतलब information matter करने लगती है।

board_events.text: Independent Is NOT Mutually Exclusive
The single biggest trap in this whole topic.
Mutually exclusive: $A \cap B = \varnothing$ — one happening forbids the other.
That is the STRONGEST dependence, not independence!
Century and a duck in the same innings: mutually exclusive, far from independent.

board_events.caption: Disjoint is not the same as independent.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 440 210" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text x="42" y="26" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#b91c1c">Mutually exclusive</text><circle cx="72" cy="108" r="42" fill="#fca5a5" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="152" cy="108" r="42" fill="#fca5a5" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="64" y="113" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#7f1d1d">A</text><text x="144" y="113" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#7f1d1d">B</text><text x="70" y="178" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#7f1d1d">no overlap</text><text x="298" y="26" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#15803d">Independent</text><circle cx="300" cy="108" r="48" fill="#86efac" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#15803d" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="360" cy="108" r="48" fill="#86efac" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#15803d" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="276" y="113" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#14532d">A</text><text x="384" y="113" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#14532d">B</text><text x="292" y="178" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#14532d">overlap = P(A)P(B)</text></svg>

board_events.text: With replacement creates independence; without replacement creates dependence.
This product form is the safe test — it never divides by zero.

segments.text: Here is where almost everyone stumbles, so let's nail it down right now.
Students hear 'independent' and 'mutually exclusive' and blur them together. They are nearly opposite ideas.
Mutually exclusive means the events can't both happen; their intersection is empty. If one occurs, the other is ruled out.
<excited>But that's the strongest possible dependence, not independence!</excited> One event completely controls the other's fate.
A batsman scoring a century and getting a duck in the same innings are mutually exclusive, about as far from independent as two events can get.
Visually, mutually exclusive events are two separate circles that never touch; independent events overlap by exactly the product of their probabilities.
A practical tell for exams: drawing with replacement leaves the box unchanged, so the draws are independent. Without replacement the box changes, and the draws become dependent.
The working definition of independence is the product rule: probability of E-and-F equals probability of E times probability of F.
Prefer this product form as your test. It never divides by anything, so it stays valid even when a probability is zero.
यहीं लगभग सब लड़खड़ाते हैं, तो इसे अभी पक्का कर लेते हैं।
Students 'independent' और 'mutually exclusive' को एक कर देते हैं। ये लगभग opposite ideas हैं।
Mutually exclusive मतलब दोनों events एक साथ हो ही नहीं सकते; उनका intersection empty है। एक हुआ तो दूसरा out।
<excited>पर ये तो सबसे strong dependence है, independence नहीं!</excited> एक event दूसरे की क़िस्मत पूरी तरह control कर रहा है।
एक ही innings में batsman का century और duck mutually exclusive हैं, independent से जितना दूर हो सकते हैं उतने।
Visually, mutually exclusive events दो अलग circles हैं जो कभी नहीं छूते; independent events बिल्कुल probabilities के product जितना overlap करते हैं।
Exam का practical tell: with replacement में box वैसा ही रहता है, तो draws independent। Without replacement में box बदलता है, और draws dependent हो जाते हैं।
Independence की working definition product rule है: probability of E-and-F बराबर probability of E गुणा probability of F।
इसी product form को test बनाओ। ये कभी किसी से भाग नहीं देता, इसलिए probability zero होने पर भी valid रहता है।

sections.title: Proof: why conditioning shrinks the sample space

board_events.text: Proof — Conditioning Shrinks the Sample Space
Claim: if $P(F) > 0$, then $P(E \mid F) = \dfrac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)}$.
Take equally likely outcomes. Knowing $F$ occurred, the effective space is $F$ alone.
Now divide top and bottom by $n(S)$, the total number of outcomes.
Dividing by $n(S)$ turns raw counts into probabilities.
That last step is why the result holds even when outcomes aren't equally likely.

segments.text: Let's prove the formula rather than just trust it. The proof is the intuition made exact.
The claim: whenever the probability of F is positive, probability of E given F equals probability of E-and-F over probability of F.
Start with equally likely outcomes. Once you know F occurred, every outcome outside F is ruled out, so your effective sample space is F alone.
Among the outcomes in F, the ones that also make E true are exactly those in E-and-F. So the conditional is the count of E-and-F over the count of F.
Here is the one clever move: divide both the top and the bottom by n of S, the total number of outcomes.
The counts become probabilities: E-and-F over F, each as a fraction of the whole. The n of S cancels, leaving our formula.
That division is the crucial step; it converts raw counts into genuine probabilities.
And because it's now written purely in probabilities, we take it as the definition even when outcomes aren't equally likely. The formula survives.
Formula को सिर्फ मानने के बजाय prove करते हैं। Proof ही intuition का exact रूप है।
Claim: जब भी probability of F positive हो, probability of E given F बराबर probability of E-and-F बटा probability of F।
Equally likely outcomes से शुरू करो। जैसे ही पता चला F हुआ, F के बाहर का हर outcome out, तो effective sample space सिर्फ F रह गया।
F के outcomes में से जो E को भी true करते हैं वो बिल्कुल E-and-F वाले हैं। तो conditional है count of E-and-F बटा count of F।
यहाँ एक clever move है: ऊपर और नीचे दोनों को n of S से divide करो, यानी total outcomes से।
Counts अब probabilities बन जाते हैं: E-and-F बटा F, हर एक पूरे का fraction। n of S cancel, और हमारा formula बचा।
यही division crucial step है; raw counts को genuine probabilities में बदल देता है।
और अब चूँकि ये पूरी तरह probabilities में लिखा है, इसे definition मान लेते हैं, तब भी जब outcomes equally likely न हों। Formula टिका रहता है।

board_events.text: Proof — Independence Survives Complements
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, so are $A$ and $B'$.
Split $A$ by whether $B$ happens or not:
So $A$ and $B'$ are independent — a CBSE favourite.
Apply twice: $A'$ with $B$, and $A'$ with $B'$, are independent too.

segments.text: Independence has a beautiful robustness that exams exploit constantly, so let's prove it.
The claim: if A and B are independent, then A and the complement of B are also independent.
Split A cleanly by whether B happens: the part of A inside B, plus the part of A outside B.
In symbols, probability of A equals probability of A-and-B plus probability of A-and-not-B.
Rearrange, then use independence to replace probability of A-and-B with probability of A times probability of B.
Factor out probability of A, and one minus probability of B is just probability of not-B. So probability of A-and-not-B equals probability of A times probability of not-B.
That is exactly the product rule, so A and not-B are independent. C B S E loves asking this one directly.
Apply the same argument twice and you get more: A-complement with B, and A-complement with B-complement, are independent too. Independence survives every complement combination.
Independence में एक सुंदर robustness है जिसे exams बार-बार use करते हैं, तो इसे prove करते हैं।
Claim: अगर A और B independent हैं, तो A और B का complement भी independent हैं।
A को साफ़-साफ़ बाँटो इस आधार पे कि B हुआ या नहीं: A का हिस्सा B के अंदर, और A का हिस्सा B के बाहर।
Symbols में, probability of A बराबर probability of A-and-B जोड़ probability of A-and-not-B।
Rearrange करो, फिर independence से probability of A-and-B को बदलो probability of A गुणा probability of B से।
probability of A बाहर निकालो, और one minus probability of B तो बस probability of not-B है। तो probability of A-and-not-B बराबर probability of A गुणा probability of not-B।
यही तो product rule है, तो A और not-B independent। C B S E इसे सीधे पूछना पसंद करता है।
यही argument दो बार लगाओ और और मिलता है: A-complement के साथ B, और A-complement के साथ B-complement, भी independent। Independence हर complement combination में टिकती है।

sections.title: Core formulas: conditional, multiplication, chain rule

board_events.text: Core Formulas — Conditional & Multiplication
Rearrange it and you get the multiplication theorem.

board_events.latex: P(E \cap F) = P(F)\,P(E \mid F) = P(E)\,P(F \mid E)

board_events.text: Two ways to build the same intersection — use whichever conditional is easier.

board_events.latex: P(E \cap F \cap G) = P(E)\,P(F \mid E)\,P(G \mid E \cap F)

board_events.text: Chain rule: condition each new event on all the previous ones.
A conditional probability is still a probability: $0 \le P(E \mid F) \le 1$.

segments.text: Let's consolidate the toolkit for this subtopic. Here is your complete set of core formulas.
First, the definition: probability of E given F is probability of E-and-F over probability of F, valid whenever the probability of F isn't zero.
Multiply both sides by probability of F and the definition turns into something you'll use everywhere, the multiplication theorem.
Probability of E-and-F equals probability of F times probability of E given F; or, conditioning the other way, probability of E times probability of F given E.
Both give the same intersection, so pick the direction whose conditional is easier to find. That choice alone saves time in exams.
For three events, chain them: probability of E-and-F-and-G is probability of E, times F given E, times G given E-and-F.
The pattern is clean: each new event is conditioned on everything that came before it.
One handy property: the complement of E given F is just one minus probability of E given F.
That works because a conditional probability is a genuine probability; it always sits between zero and one.
इस subtopic का toolkit consolidate करते हैं। ये रहा तुम्हारा core formulas का पूरा set।
पहले definition: probability of E given F बराबर probability of E-and-F बटा probability of F, valid जब तक probability of F zero न हो।
दोनों तरफ़ probability of F से multiply करो और definition बन जाती है वो चीज़ जो हर जगह काम आएगी, multiplication theorem।
Probability of E-and-F बराबर probability of F गुणा probability of E given F; या दूसरी तरफ़ condition करके, probability of E गुणा probability of F given E।
दोनों वही intersection देते हैं, तो वो direction चुनो जिसका conditional आसानी से मिले। यही choice exam में time बचाती है।
तीन events के लिए chain करो: probability of E-and-F-and-G बराबर probability of E, गुणा F given E, गुणा G given E-and-F।
Pattern साफ़ है: हर नया event उससे पहले वाले सब पे conditioned होता है।
एक handy property: complement of E given F बस one minus probability of E given F है।
ये इसलिए चलता है क्योंकि conditional probability एक genuine probability है; हमेशा zero और one के बीच।

sections.title: Independence and 'at least one of n'

board_events.text: Independence & 'At Least One'
The working definition — equivalent to $P(E \mid F) = P(E)$.
For three events, checking the pairs is NOT enough.
Mutual independence needs the triple product too, not just the pairs.
'At least one of $n$ independent events' — go through the complement 'none.'
Converts an ugly union into a clean product.

segments.text: Now the independence formulas, plus the single most-used result in the whole chapter.
The working definition: E and F are independent exactly when probability of E-and-F equals probability of E times probability of F.
This is equivalent to saying probability of E given F equals probability of E, the condition doesn't move the number, but the product form is safer to use.
A warning for three events: verifying that the three pairs are independent is not enough on its own.
You also need the triple product: probability of A-and-B-and-C equal to the product of all three individual probabilities.
Only with all four conditions, the three pairs and the triple, do you have genuine mutual independence. J E E Advanced tests exactly this gap.
Finally, the workhorse. For 'at least one of n independent events,' never expand the union. Go through the complement, 'none of them occurs.'
So probability of at least one equals one minus the product, over all events, of one minus each event's probability.
That single trick converts an awkward union with many cross-terms into a clean product. Reach for it whenever you see 'at least one.'
अब independence के formulas, और पूरे chapter का सबसे ज़्यादा use होने वाला result।
Working definition: E और F independent हैं ठीक तब जब probability of E-and-F बराबर हो probability of E गुणा probability of F के।
ये कहने के बराबर है कि probability of E given F बराबर probability of E, condition number नहीं हिलाता, पर product form use करना safer है।
तीन events के लिए warning: तीनों pairs का independent होना अकेले काफ़ी नहीं।
triple product भी चाहिए: probability of A-and-B-and-C बराबर तीनों individual probabilities के product के।
चारों conditions के साथ ही, तीन pairs और triple, genuine mutual independence मिलती है। J E E Advanced यही gap test करता है।
आख़िर में workhorse। 'At least one of n independent events' के लिए union कभी expand मत करो। Complement से जाओ, 'कोई भी नहीं होता'।
तो probability of at least one बराबर one minus वो product, सारे events पे, one minus हर event की probability का।
यही एक trick एक awkward union को, ढेर सारे cross-terms वाले, clean product में बदल देती है। जब भी 'at least one' दिखे, इसे उठाओ।

sections.title: Worked example: conditional on a die (CBSE)

board_events.text: Worked Example — Conditional on a Die (CBSE)
A fair die is rolled twice. $E$: sum is $9$. $F$: first roll exceeds $3$.
Total outcomes: $36$. $F$ means first roll in $\{4,5,6\}$.
$E \cap F$: sum $9$ with first roll above $3$ — pairs $(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)$.
$(3,6)$ is rejected — a first roll of $3$ is not greater than $3$.

segments.text: Let's run a clean Boards-level problem end to end.
A fair die is rolled twice. E is the event that the sum is nine; F is the event that the first roll shows a number greater than three.
There are thirty six equally likely outcomes. F fixes the first roll to four, five, or six.
That's three choices for the first roll and six for the second, so probability of F is eighteen over thirty six.
Now E-and-F: sum nine with the first roll above three. The pairs are four-five, five-four, and six-three.
<whisper>Watch the trap: three-six is rejected, because a first roll of three is not greater than three.</whisper> That is the mark most students drop.
So there are three good outcomes, giving probability of E-and-F equal to three over thirty six.
Divide: three over thirty six, over eighteen over thirty six, gives one over six. That is your conditional probability.
एक साफ़ Boards-level problem पूरा चलाते हैं।
एक fair die दो बार roll होती है। E event है कि sum nine हो; F event है कि पहला roll three से बड़ा हो।
छत्तीस equally likely outcomes हैं। F पहले roll को four, five, या six पे fix कर देता है।
यानी पहले roll के तीन choices और दूसरे के six, तो probability of F है अठारह बटा छत्तीस।
अब E-and-F: sum nine और पहला roll three से ऊपर। Pairs हैं four-five, five-four, और six-three।
<whisper>Trap देखो: three-six reject है, क्योंकि पहला roll three, three से बड़ा नहीं।</whisper> यहीं ज़्यादातर students marks गँवाते हैं।
तो तीन अच्छे outcomes, probability of E-and-F बराबर तीन बटा छत्तीस।
Divide करो: तीन बटा छत्तीस, बटा अठारह बटा छत्तीस, बराबर one बटा six। यही तुम्हारी conditional probability।

sections.title: Worked example: independent or exclusive? (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Worked Example — Independent or Exclusive? (JEE Main)
$P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$. Classify $A$ and $B$.
Don't guess from the setup — get the intersection first.

board_events.latex: P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)

board_events.text: Independence test: $P(A)\,P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.2$.
Not mutually exclusive: $P(A \cap B) = 0.2 \neq 0$.

segments.text: This is a classic J E E Main speed trap. One line of work saves you from a wrong reflex.
You're given probability of A is zero point five, probability of B is zero point four, and probability of A-or-B is zero point seven. Are they independent, mutually exclusive, both, or neither?
Don't panic-list cases. The move is to find probability of A-and-B first, in a single line.
Use the addition theorem: probability of A-and-B equals probability of A plus probability of B minus probability of A-or-B.
That is zero point five plus zero point four minus zero point seven, which is zero point two.
Now test independence: probability of A times probability of B is zero point five times zero point four, again zero point two.
Since probability of A-and-B equals the product, A and B are independent.

<excited>And they're not mutually exclusive!</excited> That would need the intersection to be zero, but it's zero point two. The trap is assuming exclusivity from a tidy setup; always compute the intersection first.
ये classic J E E Main speed trap है। एक line का काम तुम्हें ग़लत reflex से बचा लेता है।
दिया है probability of A है zero point five, probability of B है zero point four, और probability of A-or-B है zero point seven। ये independent हैं, mutually exclusive, दोनों, या कोई नहीं?
Cases मत गिनने लगो। सही move है probability of A-and-B पहले निकालो, एक ही line में।
Addition theorem use करो: probability of A-and-B बराबर probability of A जोड़ probability of B घटा probability of A-or-B।
यानी zero point five जोड़ zero point four घटा zero point seven, जो है zero point two।
अब independence test: probability of A गुणा probability of B है zero point five गुणा zero point four, फिर से zero point two।
चूँकि probability of A-and-B product के बराबर है, A और B independent हैं।
<excited>और mutually exclusive नहीं हैं!</excited> उसके लिए intersection zero चाहिए था, पर वो zero point two है। Trap है tidy setup से exclusivity मान लेना; हमेशा intersection पहले निकालो।

sections.title: Worked example: picking without replacement (JEE Main)

board_events.text: Worked Example — Picking Without Replacement (JEE Main)
Panel: $7$ boys, $5$ girls. Pick $3$ one by one, no replacement.
(i) Given the first two are girls, chance the third is a boy?
Two girls removed leaves $10$ people, of whom $7$ are boys.
(ii) Chance all three picks are girls — use the chain rule.

board_events.latex: P(G_1 \cap G_2 \cap G_3) = P(G_1)\,P(G_2 \mid G_1)\,P(G_3 \mid G_1 \cap G_2)

board_events.text: Each factor uses the shrunken pool from the pick before it.

segments.text: Here is where the chain rule earns its keep: a without-replacement selection.
A panel has seven boys and five girls. Three members are picked one after another, without replacement.
Part one: given that the first two picked are girls, what's the chance the third pick is a boy?
Once two girls are gone, ten people remain, and seven of them are boys.
By the reduced-sample-space idea, the chance the third is a boy is simply seven over ten.
Part two asks for the chance all three picks are girls. This is a job for the chain rule.
Probability of girl, then girl, then girl is probability of the first girl, times the second given the first, times the third given the first two.
That is five twelfths times four elevenths times three tenths, which simplifies to one over twenty two.
Notice each factor uses the shrunken pool left by the pick before it; that shrinking is exactly what 'without replacement' means.
यहाँ chain rule अपनी क़ीमत वसूल करता है: एक without-replacement selection।
एक panel में सात boys और पाँच girls हैं। तीन members एक-एक करके चुने जाते हैं, without replacement।
Part one: दिया कि पहले दो girls हैं, तीसरा pick boy होने का chance क्या है?
दो girls जाने के बाद दस लोग बचते हैं, और उनमें सात boys हैं।
Reduced-sample-space idea से, तीसरा boy होने का chance बस सात बटा दस।
Part two पूछता है तीनों picks girls होने का chance। ये chain rule का काम है।
Probability of girl, फिर girl, फिर girl बराबर पहली girl की probability, गुणा दूसरी first के given, गुणा तीसरी पहली दो के given।
यानी five twelfths गुणा four elevenths गुणा three tenths, जो simplify होकर one बटा twenty two।
ध्यान दो हर factor उससे पहले वाले pick से बची छोटी pool use करता है; यही shrinking 'without replacement' का मतलब है।

sections.title: Worked example: both, neither, exactly one (JEE Advanced)

board_events.text: Worked Example — Both, Neither, Exactly One (JEE Advanced)
$A$, $B$ independent. $P(\text{both}) = \tfrac{1}{8}$, $P(\text{neither}) = \tfrac{3}{8}$.
Let $P(A) = a$, $P(B) = b$. Independence gives $ab = \tfrac{1}{8}$.
So $a, b$ are roots of $8t^2 - 6t + 1 = 0$.
Exactly one occurs: $P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B)$.
Check: $\tfrac{1}{8} + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{3}{8} = 1$ — the three cases exhaust everything.

segments.text: Now a full J E E Advanced build; it stitches several ideas together.
A and B are independent. The probability both occur is one eighth, and the probability neither occurs is three eighths. Find the two probabilities and the chance exactly one occurs.
Let probability of A be a and probability of B be b. Independence immediately gives a times b equals one eighth.
For 'neither,' remember the complements are also independent, so probability of neither is one minus a, times one minus b, equal to three eighths.
Expand: one, minus the sum of a and b, plus a-b, equals three eighths. Substitute a-b as one eighth and you get a plus b equals three quarters.
Now a and b are the two roots of the quadratic eight t squared minus six t plus one equals zero.
Solving, t equals six plus or minus two, over sixteen, which is one half or one quarter. So the pair is one half and one quarter.
Finally, 'exactly one occurs' is probability of A plus probability of B minus twice the probability of both.
That is three quarters minus two times one eighth, which is one half.

<whisper>Always run this check:</whisper> both, plus exactly one, plus neither, one eighth, one half, three eighths, sums to one. Those three cases exhaust every possibility, so the answer is consistent.
अब एक पूरा J E E Advanced build; ये कई ideas को जोड़ता है।
A और B independent हैं। दोनों होने की probability one eighth, और कोई भी न होने की probability three eighths। दोनों probabilities और exactly one होने का chance निकालो।
मानो probability of A है a और probability of B है b। Independence तुरंत देता है a गुणा b बराबर one eighth।
'Neither' के लिए याद रखो complements भी independent हैं, तो probability of neither है one minus a, गुणा one minus b, बराबर three eighths।
Expand करो: one, घटा a और b का sum, जोड़ a-b, बराबर three eighths। a-b को one eighth रखो और मिलता है a जोड़ b बराबर three quarters।
अब a और b उस quadratic के दो roots हैं: eight t squared minus six t plus one बराबर zero।
Solve करने पर, t बराबर six plus-or-minus two, बटा sixteen, जो है one half या one quarter। तो pair है one half और one quarter।
आख़िर में, 'exactly one occurs' है probability of A जोड़ probability of B घटा दो गुना probability of both।
यानी three quarters घटा दो गुना one eighth, जो है one half।

<whisper>ये check हमेशा चलाओ:</whisper> both, जोड़ exactly one, जोड़ neither, one eighth, one half, three eighths, का sum one है। ये तीनों cases हर possibility को cover करते हैं, तो answer consistent है।

board_events.text: Common Pitfalls — Read Before the Exam
Pitfall 1: confusing 'mutually exclusive' with 'independent.'
Mutually exclusive with positive probabilities means strongly dependent, not independent.
Pitfall 2: flipping the conditional — $P(A \mid B) \neq P(B \mid A)$.
Umbrella given rain is high; rain given umbrella is much lower — same events.
Pitfall 3: pairwise independence does NOT imply mutual independence.
For three events, the triple product can still fail even if all pairs pass.
Pitfall 4: ignoring the given, reverting to the unconditional probability.
In 'given at least one girl,' using the plain probability throws away the condition.

segments.text: Let's lock in the four traps that cost the most marks in this subtopic.
Pitfall one, the big one: confusing mutually exclusive with independent.
Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are strongly dependent; one happening forbids the other. That is the opposite of independence, not a version of it.
Pitfall two: flipping the conditional. Probability of A given B is generally not probability of B given A; their denominators differ.
Feel it: the chance someone carries an umbrella given it's raining is high, but the chance it's raining given they carry an umbrella is much lower. Same two events, very different numbers.
Pitfall three: assuming pairwise independence gives you mutual independence.
For three events, all three pairs can be independent and yet the triple product condition still fails. Check the triple explicitly.
Pitfall four: ignoring the information you were given, and sliding back to the unconditional probability.
In a problem that says 'given at least one girl,' quoting the plain probability throws away the very condition that defines the question.
इस subtopic में सबसे ज़्यादा marks खाने वाले चार traps पक्के कर लेते हैं।
Pitfall one, सबसे बड़ा: mutually exclusive को independent समझ लेना।
Positive probabilities वाले mutually exclusive events strongly dependent हैं; एक हुआ तो दूसरा मना। ये independence का opposite है, उसका version नहीं।
Pitfall two: conditional flip कर देना। Probability of A given B आम तौर पे probability of B given A नहीं होती; उनके denominators अलग हैं।
Feel करो: बारिश के given कोई umbrella रखता है इसका chance high है, पर umbrella के given बारिश हो रही है ये chance बहुत कम। वही दो events, बहुत अलग numbers।
Pitfall three: pairwise independence से mutual independence मान लेना।
तीन events के लिए तीनों pairs independent हो सकते हैं फिर भी triple product condition fail कर सकती है। Triple explicitly check करो।
Pitfall four: दी गई information ignore करके unconditional probability पे फिसल जाना।
'Given at least one girl' वाली problem में plain probability बोलना उसी condition को फेंक देता है जो सवाल को define करती है।

board_events.text: Phrase-to-Symbol Decoder + Pro-Tip
Translate exam English into set notation before touching a formula.
'given that $F$ has occurred' $\to$ a conditional $P(\cdot \mid F)$.
'both $A$ and $B$' $\to P(A \cap B)$; '$A$ or $B$' $\to P(A \cup B)$.
'neither $A$ nor $B$' $\to P(A' \cap B') = 1 - P(A \cup B)$.

board_events.latex: P(\text{exactly one of } A, B) = P(A) + P(B) - 2P(A \cap B)

board_events.text: Pro-tip: compute the intersection first, then run two one-second checks.
Is $P(A \cap B) = 0$? Is $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)$?
'$= 0$' means mutually exclusive; '$= P(A)P(B)$' means independent.

segments.text: Close the subtopic with the single most reliable exam habit: decode the words first.
Half the battle in probability is translating exam English into set notation before you reach for any formula.
When you see 'given that F has occurred,' or 'if it is known that F,' that's a conditional; the denominator becomes probability of F.
'Both A and B' is intersection; 'A or B,' or 'at least one of A and B,' is union.
'Neither A nor B' is the intersection of the complements, which equals one minus probability of A-or-B.
And 'exactly one of A and B' is probability of A plus probability of B minus twice their intersection; remember the factor of two.
<whisper>Here is the pro-tip that resolves almost every classification question:</whisper> compute the intersection first, then run two one-second checks.
Ask: is the intersection zero? And is it equal to probability of A times probability of B?

If it's zero they're mutually exclusive; if it equals the product they're independent, and they can never both be yes unless a probability is zero. Write the symbols in the margin first and the right formula becomes obvious.
Subtopic को सबसे भरोसेमंद exam habit से बंद करते हैं: पहले words को decode करो।
Probability में आधी लड़ाई exam English को formula छूने से पहले set notation में translate करने की है।
जब 'given that F has occurred', या 'if it is known that F' दिखे, वो conditional है; denominator बन जाता है probability of F।
'Both A and B' intersection है; 'A or B', या 'at least one of A and B', union है।
'Neither A nor B' complements का intersection है, जो बराबर है one minus probability of A-or-B।
और 'exactly one of A and B' है probability of A जोड़ probability of B घटा दो गुना उनका intersection; factor of two याद रखो।
<whisper>ये रहा pro-tip जो लगभग हर classification question सुलझा देता है:</whisper> intersection पहले निकालो, फिर दो one-second checks चलाओ।
पूछो: क्या intersection zero है? और क्या ये probability of A गुणा probability of B के बराबर है?

अगर zero है तो mutually exclusive; अगर product के बराबर है तो independent, और दोनों कभी yes नहीं हो सकते जब तक कोई probability zero न हो। Symbols पहले margin में लिखो और सही formula obvious हो जाता है।
